lessons.title: Promoter Holding: What High, Low and Falling Stakes Signal

body.text: Promoter holding tells you how much of the promoter's own money rides alongside yours. The level matters less than the direction, and the direction matters less than the reason.

children.text: In most Indian listed companies, a founder family, a parent company, or the government controls the board. That controlling group is the promoter, and its stake is the single most checked governance number on screener.in. It is also one of the most misread. A 70% stake can hide a promoter extracting value through related parties. A 5% stake can sit on top of one of the best-run companies in the country. This lesson teaches you to read the number properly.

Under Regulation 31 of SEBI's LODR Regulations, every listed company files its shareholding pattern with BSE and NSE within 21 days of the end of each quarter. The filing splits owners into the promoter and promoter group, and the public, which is further split into institutions such as mutual funds, FPIs and insurers, and non-institutions such as retail investors. Screener.in summarises this into Promoters, FIIs, DIIs, Government and Public, with a quarterly history you can scroll back through for years.

body.label: BSE Corporate Filings
body.description: Search the company, open its Shareholding Pattern for any quarter, and expand the promoter table to see each promoter entity by name, its share count, and shares pledged or encumbered.

children.text: The Thresholds That Change Who Controls What

markDefs.definition: A resolution that needs votes in favour to be at least three times the votes against, which works out to 75% of votes cast. Required for changes such as altering the articles of association or certain capital raises.

children.text: Promoter holding is not a smooth scale. A few specific percentages change what the promoter can do without you. Under the Companies Act, 2013, an ordinary resolution needs a simple majority of votes cast, while a
needs 75% of votes cast. SEBI's takeover rules and minimum public shareholding norms add further lines.

body.caption: Key promoter holding thresholds in Indian listed companies

cells: More than 25%
Can block special resolutions on its own if it votes against. Acquiring 25% or more triggers a mandatory open offer
Companies Act, 2013; SEBI SAST Regulations, 2011
More than 50%
Controls every ordinary resolution: appointing directors, approving accounts, dividends
Companies Act, 2013
Can increase the stake by up to 5% per financial year without an open offer, known as creeping acquisition
SEBI SAST Regulations, 2011
Effective ceiling. At least 25% must be held by the public, so a promoter above 75% must sell down within the permitted time
Minimum public shareholding, Rule 19A of the SCRR

body.text: A promoter at 51% controls the board just as firmly as one at 74%. Above 50%, a higher stake adds alignment, not control. That is why the extra percentage points are worth reading as skin in the game rather than power.

children.text: High, Low, or None: What the Level Tells You

body.caption: Reading the level of promoter holding

cells: Family-run mid caps, MNC subsidiaries such as Nestle India and Hindustan Unilever, PSUs
Promoter's wealth is heavily tied to the share price, so incentives align with yours
Minority shareholders have little voice; value can leak through royalties and related party deals that a controlling holder can push through
Many established family businesses after several fund raises
Promoter retains practical control but has diluted to fund growth
If combined with high pledging, a falling share price can threaten control and trigger distress selling
Below 25%
Promoters who diluted through many equity raises, or have been selling steadily
Can reflect a mature company where institutions own the majority
Promoter may control the board with little of their own money at stake
No promoter
ITC, Larsen & Toubro, ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank after its 2023 merger with HDFC Ltd
Board and management answer to a dispersed, largely institutional shareholder base
Management can become entrenched with no owner to challenge it; check pay, board independence, and capital allocation closely

children.text: Notice that no level is automatically good or bad. High promoter holding aligns incentives but concentrates power. No promoter spreads power but removes the owner who cares most. The level tells you which risks to go looking for in the rest of this course.
The Percentage Can Move Without the Promoter Doing Anything

This is the most common mistake investors make with this number. Promoter holding is a percentage, so it changes whenever the total share count changes. A QIP, a preferential issue to investors, or ESOP allotments add shares and push the promoter percentage down with no selling at all. A buyback in which the promoter does not tender its shares reduces the share count and pushes the promoter percentage up with no buying at all. Before you react to a change on screener.in, check the actual number of shares the promoter group holds.

body.latex: \text{Promoter Holding (\%)} = \frac{\text{Shares held by promoter group}}{\text{Total shares outstanding}} \times 100

body.title: The Buyback Effect
body.prompt: A promoter group holds 45 crore shares out of 90 crore shares outstanding, a 50% stake. The company buys back and extinguishes 10 crore shares, and the promoter group does not tender any of its shares. What is the promoter holding percentage after the buyback? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Promoter shares stay at 45 crore. Total shares fall to 90 - 10 = 80 crore. Holding = 45 ÷ 80 × 100 = 56.25%. The stake rose by 6.25 percentage points without the promoter buying a single share, so this is not a sign of fresh promoter confidence.

body.text: Screener.in's shareholding section shows percentages. Always check whether the promoter group's share count changed before calling a move a 'promoter sale' or a 'promoter buy'. The detailed shareholding pattern on BSE or NSE shows the share count for every promoter entity.

children.text: When the Promoter Really Is Selling: Read the Reason

Promoters sell for many reasons, and most are not sinister. The skill is separating one-off, explained sales from steady, unexplained ones. Under SEBI's insider trading rules, promoters must disclose trades worth more than ₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter within two trading days, and the company must pass that disclosure to the exchanges within two trading days of receiving it. Under the takeover rules, any change of 2% or more in a promoter's holding also has to be disclosed. So you can see sales as they happen, not just at quarter end.

columns.label: Usually Benign
points: Selling to meet the 25% minimum public shareholding requirement
A single, announced block deal or Offer for Sale with a stated purpose such as family succession or philanthropy
Stake reduced by a few points after a large run-up, with no pledging and no change in the business
Share count falls only because of QIP or ESOP dilution

columns.label: Worth Worrying About
points: Small, steady open market sales quarter after quarter with no explanation
Selling while management guides for strong growth on the concall
Sales alongside rising pledges or loans from the company to promoter entities
Selling just before weak results, a regulatory action, or an auditor change

children.text: Go back to Satyam in Lesson 3. The Raju family's stake drifted down from over 25% to under 9% across most of a decade while the company reported strong profits and a growing cash pile. Any one year looked explainable. The seven-year trend, next to a promoter who claimed the business was flush with cash, was not.

Promoter buying deserves the same scrutiny in reverse. Genuine open market purchases or creeping acquisition with the promoter's own money are a strong signal of confidence. An increase that comes from a buyback, or from warrants issued to the promoter at a price below the market, is not the same thing, and the second is covered as a dilution red flag in Chapter 5.

body.title: What Changed?
body.question: On screener.in, a company's promoter holding moves from 52.0% to 48.5% in one quarter. The BSE shareholding pattern shows the promoter group holds exactly the same number of shares in both quarters. What most likely happened?
options: The promoter sold shares through a block deal
The company issued new shares, for example through a QIP, preferential issue, or ESOP allotment
The company completed a buyback in which the promoter did not participate
body.explanation: With the promoter's share count unchanged, the percentage can only fall if total shares outstanding increased. That points to fresh issuance. A block deal or pledge invocation would reduce the promoter's share count, and a buyback without promoter participation would push the percentage up, not down.

body.title: Two Promoters, Two Sales
body.scenario: Company P: after the stock tripled in three years, the promoter family sells 4% of the company in a single block deal on NSE, taking its stake from 59% to 55%. The exchange filing states the proceeds will fund a family charitable foundation. No promoter shares are pledged. Company Q: the promoter stake has slipped from 48% to 41% over eight quarters through small open market sales of 0.5% to 1% each quarter. There is no explanation in any filing. On the latest concall, the CEO guided for 30% revenue growth and called the stock 'deeply undervalued'.
body.prompt: Which sale concerns you more, and what would you check next for each company?
body.modelAnswer: Company Q is the bigger concern. The sales are steady, unexplained, and directly contradict management's own claim that the stock is undervalued. If the promoter truly believed the stock was cheap, they would not be selling every quarter. For Q, check for pledged shares, loans or advances from the company to promoter entities, related party transactions, and whether the selling picked up before any results. For Company P, the sale is a single, disclosed event with a stated purpose, after a large price rise, with no pledging and a stake still well above 50%. Check that no further sales follow in the next few quarters and that the stated use of proceeds matches what happens. One explained sale is a data point. A pattern of unexplained sales that contradicts management's words is a signal.

body.title: Advanced: when promoters stop being promoters

children.text: Under Regulation 31A of the LODR Regulations, a promoter can apply to be reclassified as a public shareholder. The conditions include holding no more than 10% of the company, having no special rights or board seat, and not acting as a key managerial person, with approval from the board, shareholders, and the stock exchanges. A promoter exiting after selling down is normal. But watch for reclassification in companies where the outgoing promoter still has close business dealings with the company, because related party rules then stop applying to them in the same way.

body.title: Read Promoter Holding for One of Your Stocks
steps: Open the company on screener.in and switch the shareholding section to quarterly; note the promoter percentage over the last 12 quarters
For any quarter where it moved by more than 1 percentage point, open that quarter's shareholding pattern on BSE and compare the promoter group's share count with the previous quarter
If the share count is unchanged, find the corporate action that changed total shares: QIP, preferential issue, ESOP allotment, or buyback
If the share count fell, search the company's exchange announcements for insider trading or takeover regulation disclosures that explain the sale
Place the stake in the right band from the thresholds table and note which risks that band points you towards
Write one line: is the promoter's own money at stake rising, stable, or falling, and is there a credible reason?

body.text: Companies named in this lesson illustrate ownership structures and are used for education only. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Shareholding patterns are filed quarterly under LODR Regulation 31 within 21 days of quarter end, and are summarised on screener.in
Key thresholds: above 25% can block special resolutions, above 50% controls ordinary resolutions, and 75% is the effective ceiling under minimum public shareholding rules
No level is automatically good: high holding aligns incentives but concentrates power, and no promoter spreads power but can entrench management
Promoter percentage moves with the total share count, so QIPs and ESOPs lower it and buybacks raise it without any trading by the promoter
Always check the promoter group's share count on BSE or NSE before reading a change as a sale or a purchase
One explained sale is normal; steady, unexplained selling that contradicts management's optimism is a warning sign
